<!-- theorem--1: body_md -->
Let $\Delta$ be a thick irreducible right-angled building over an index set $I$ with $\lvert I \rvert \geq 2$. Let $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ and $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ be the local data as in \cref{def:restricted2}. Assume that $F_i = \acute F_i$ for every $i\in I$ that is the type of a rung. Moreover, assume that not all local groups $\acute F_i$ are free.            
	
	Then the restricted universal group $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is virtually simple if and only if $\acute F_i$ is generated by point stabilizers for every $i\in I$ and transitive for every $i$ in some vertex cover of the diagram of $\Delta$.
<!-- end theorem--1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:coloring}
	Let $\Delta$ be a semiregular right-angled building of type~$M$ over $I$ with parameters $(q_i)_{i \in I}$.
	For each $i\in I$, consider a set $\Omega_i$ of cardinality~$q_i$, the elements of which we call \emph{$i$-colors} or \emph{$i$-labels}.
	A \emph{legal coloring} of~$\Delta$ (with color sets $\Omega_i$) is a map
	\[ \lambda\colon \Delta\to\prod_{i\in I} \Omega_i\colon c\mapsto(\lambda_i(c))_{i\in I} \]
	satisfying the following properties for every $i\in I$ and for every $i$-panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item the restriction $\mathchoice{{\lambda_i\bigr\rvert_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{}}}{{\lambda_i\rvert_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{}}}{{\lambda_i\rvert_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{}}}{{\lambda_i\rvert_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{}}}\colon \ensuremath\mathcal{P}\to\Omega_i$ is a bijection;
		\item for every $j\neq i$, the restriction $\mathchoice{{\lambda_j\bigr\rvert_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{}}}{{\lambda_j\rvert_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{}}}{{\lambda_j\rvert_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{}}}{{\lambda_j\rvert_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{}}}\colon \ensuremath\mathcal{P}\to\Omega_j$ is a constant map.
	\end{enumerate}
	                                                                                                                                                                           
    By \cite[Proposition 2.44]{silva1}, such a legal coloring is essentially unique.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:universal}
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item 
            Consider an automorphism $g\in\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ and an arbitrary $i$-panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$. Then we define the \emph{local action of $g$ at $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$} as the map
        	\[\sigma_\lambda(g,\ensuremath\mathcal{P}) = \mathchoice{{\lambda_i\bigr\rvert_{g\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{}}}{{\lambda_i\rvert_{g\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{}}}{{\lambda_i\rvert_{g\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{}}}{{\lambda_i\rvert_{g\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{}}} \circ \mathchoice{{g\bigr\rvert_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{}}}{{g\rvert_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{}}}{{g\rvert_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{}}}{{g\rvert_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{}}} \circ \mathchoice{{\lambda_i\bigr\rvert_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{-1}}}{{\lambda_i\rvert_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{-1}}}{{\lambda_i\rvert_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{-1}}}{{\lambda_i\rvert_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}^{-1}}}, \]
        	which is a permutation of $\Omega_i$ by definition of $\lambda$.
        	In other words, the local action $\sigma_\lambda(g,\ensuremath\mathcal{P})$ is the map that makes the following diagram commute.
        	\[\begin{tikzcd}[dims={7em}{4em}]
        		\ensuremath\mathcal{P} \ar[r,"g"] \ar[d,"\lambda_i"]
        			& g\ensuremath\mathcal{P} \ar[d,"\lambda_i"]\\
        		\Omega_i \ar[r,"{\sigma_\lambda(g,\,\ensuremath\mathcal{P})}"] & \Omega_i
        	\end{tikzcd}\]
        \item 
        	Let $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ be a collection of permutation groups $F_i\leq\operatorname{Sym}(\Omega_i)$, indexed by $i\in I$. The \emph{universal group} of $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ over $\Delta$ (with respect to $\lambda$) is the group
        	\[
        	   \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) = \bigl\{g\in\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta) \bigm| \sigma_\lambda(g,\ensuremath\mathcal{P})\in F_i  \text{ for each $i\in I$ and each $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\in\operatorname{Res}_i(\Delta)$}\bigr\},
        	\]
        	i.e., $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is the group of automorphisms that locally act like permutations in $F_i$. We call the groups $F_i$ the \emph{local groups} and we refer to the collection $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ as the \emph{local data} for $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$.
        	                                                                                                          
        	We will sometimes explicitly include the building $\Delta$ in the notation and write $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ instead.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:localcomposition}
	Let $g,h\in\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ and let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be any panel. Then the local actions satisfy
	\[\sigma_\lambda(gh,\ensuremath\mathcal{P}) = \sigma_\lambda(g,h\ensuremath\mathcal{P})\cdot\sigma_\lambda(h,\ensuremath\mathcal{P})
		\qquad\text{and}\qquad
		\sigma_\lambda(g,\ensuremath\mathcal{P})^{-1} = \sigma_\lambda(g^{-1},g\ensuremath\mathcal{P}).\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
This follows immediately from the definition.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:ext-res}
    Let $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}$ be a residue of $\Delta$ of type $J \subseteq I$. Let $g \in \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_\ensuremath\mathcal{R}(\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}})$. Then $g$ extends to an element of $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
This is \cite[Proposition 3.15]{silva1}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:harmonious}
    Let $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ be local data over $I$ and let $J \subseteq I$.
    Two $J$-residues $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}$ and $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}'$ are called \emph{harmonious} (with respect to $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$) if for each $k \in I \setminus J$, the (well-defined) colors $\lambda_k(\ensuremath\mathcal{R})$ and $\lambda_k(\ensuremath\mathcal{R}')$ lie in the same orbit of the local group $F_k$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:universalorbits}
    Two residues $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}$ and $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}'$ lie in the same orbit of $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ if and only if they are harmonious.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
This is \cite[Proposition 3.1]{bossaert}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
    \item 
        If $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_1$ and $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_2$ are residues of $\Delta$, we set
        \[\operatorname{proj}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_2}(\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_1) = \{\operatorname{proj}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_2}(c)\mid c\in\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_1\}.\]
        Note that this set is again a residue of $\Delta$ contained in $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_2$, and that its rank is bounded by the ranks of both $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_1$ and $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_2$.
    \item 
    	Two residues $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_1$ and $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_2$ of $\Delta$ are called \emph{parallel} if $\operatorname{proj}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_1}(\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_2) = \ensuremath\mathcal{R}_1$ and $\operatorname{proj}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_2}(\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_1) = \ensuremath\mathcal{R}_2$. In that case, the projection maps define bijections between $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_1$ and $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_2$.
    \item 
    	Let $J\subseteq I$. Then we define the set
    	\[J^\perp = \{i\in I\mid \text{$m_{ij}=2$ for all $j\in J$}\} = \{i\in I\setminus J \mid \text{$ij=ji$ for all $j\in J$}\}.\]
    	When $J=\{j\}$ is a singleton, we simply write $j^\perp := \{j\}^\perp$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:parallelinrab}
	Let $\Delta$ be a right-angled building over $I$.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item\label{prop:parallelinrab:1} Two parallel residues have equal type.
		\item\label{prop:parallelinrab:2} Two residues of equal type $J$ are parallel if and only if they are contained in a common residue of type $J\cup J^\perp$.
		\item\label{prop:parallelinrab:3} Parallelism of residues is an equivalence relation.
		\item\label{prop:parallelinrab:4} Two panels $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}_1$ and $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}_2$ are parallel if and only if there exist two chambers in $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}_1$ with distinct projections on $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}_2$.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
We refer to \cite[Lemma 2.5, Proposition 2.8 and Corollary 2.9]{caprace2014}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:parallellocals}
	Let $g \in \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$. If\, $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ and $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ are two parallel panels in $\Delta$, then the local actions $\sigma_\lambda(g,\ensuremath\mathcal{P})$ and $\sigma_\lambda(g,\ensuremath\mathcal{P}')$ are identical.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
This is \cite[Lemma 3.7]{bossaert}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
We define the \emph{permutation topology} on $\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ by taking as an identity neighborhood basis the collection of all pointwise stabilizers of finite subsets of $\Delta$. This makes $\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ (and all its subgroups) into a totally disconnected group.
    
    If all parameters $q_i$ are finite---this will always be the case later on---then $\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ is also locally compact, and the same is then true for the universal groups $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:young}
	\begin{enumerate}
	    \item 
        	To every partition of a set $X$, we can associate a subgroup of $\operatorname{Sym}(X)$ of all permutations stabilizing the blocks of the partition. A subgroup obtained in this fashion is called a \emph{Young subgroup} of $\operatorname{Sym}(X)$, and is naturally isomorphic to the direct product of the symmetric groups on the blocks.
	    \item 
        	For any permutation group $G\leq\operatorname{Sym}(X)$, we have a canonical partition of $X$ into $G$-orbits. We call the Young subgroup associated to this partition the \emph{Young overgroup of $G$} and denote it by $\widehat G$.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
A subset $C$ of $\Delta$ is called \emph{panel-closed} if:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $C$ is convex (i.e., if $c,d \in C$, then all chambers on all minimal galleries between $c$ and $d$ are also contained in $C$), and
        \item each panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ of $\Delta$ containing at least $2$ chambers of $C$ is completely contained in $C$.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:closingsquares}
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item \label{lem:closingsquares:1}
            Let $c, c_1, c_2, c_3 \in \Delta$ be such that $\operatorname{dist}(c,c_1) = \operatorname{dist}(c,c_3) = n$, $\operatorname{dist}(c,c_2) = n+1$, and $c_1\sim_i c_2\sim_j c_3$ for $i\neq j$. Then $m_{ij}=2$ and there exists $d\in\Delta$ such that $\operatorname{dist}(c,d) = n-1$ and $c_1\sim_j d\sim_i c_3$.
        \item \label{lem:closingsquares:2}
            Let $c, c_1, c_2, c_3 \in \Delta$ be such that $\operatorname{dist}(c,c_1) = \operatorname{dist}(c,c_2) = n+1$, $\operatorname{dist}(c,c_3) = n$, and $c_1\sim_i c_2\sim_j c_3$ for $i\neq j$. Then $m_{ij}=2$ and there exists $d\in\Delta$ such that $\operatorname{dist}(c,d) = n$ and $c_1\sim_j d\sim_i c_3$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
See \cite[Lemmas 2.9 and 2.10]{silva1}; see also \cref{fig:closingsquares} below.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:concave}
    Let $c, c_1, c_2 \in \Delta$. Then there exists a minimal gallery
    \[ \gamma = (v_0,\dots,v_\ell), \quad \text{with } v_0 = c_1,\ v_\ell = c_2, \]
    such that there are numbers $0 \leq j \leq k \leq \ell$ satisfying:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\operatorname{dist}(c, v_i) < \operatorname{dist}(c, v_{i-1})$ for all $i \in \{ 1,\dots, j \}$,
        \item $\operatorname{dist}(c, v_i) = \operatorname{dist}(c, v_{i-1})$ for all $i \in \{ j+1,\dots, k \}$,
        \item $\operatorname{dist}(c, v_i) > \operatorname{dist}(c, v_{i-1})$ for all $i \in \{ k+1,\dots, \ell \}$.
    \end{itemize}
    Such a minimal gallery from $c_1$ to $c_2$ will be called \emph{concave (with respect to $c$)}.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
This is \cite[Lemma 2.11]{silva1}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:convexgateproperty}
	Let $C$ be a panel-closed subset of $\Delta$ and let $c\in\Delta$ be any chamber. Then there is a unique chamber $d\in C$ such that $\operatorname{dist}(c,d)$ is minimal.
	Moreover, the gate property holds: for every chamber $e\in C$, there exists a minimal gallery from $c$ to $e$ passing through $d$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Assume that $d$ and $d'$ are two distinct chambers in $C$ that minimize the distance to $c$. Let $\gamma$ be the minimal gallery that joins $d$ and $d'$ and is concave with respect to $c$ (as in \cref{prop:concave}). By convexity of~$C$ and concavity of~$\gamma$, every chamber on $\gamma$ is a chamber in $C$ at the same distance to $c$ as $d$ and $d'$. We may thus assume that $d$ and $d'$ are $i$-adjacent for some $i\in I$. Let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be the $i$-panel containing $d$ and $d'$; by assumption, $\ensuremath\mathcal{P} \subseteq C$. Now let $c'=\operatorname{proj}_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}(c)$; then $\operatorname{dist}(c,c')<\operatorname{dist}(c,d)$, while $c'\in C$. This is a contradiction, showing that there is a unique chamber $d\in C$ closest to $c$.
	
	For the gate property, we use induction on $\operatorname{dist}(c,C)$. If $c\in C$, then there is nothing to show. Now assume $\operatorname{dist}(c,C)\geq 1$ and let $c'\in\Delta$ and $i\in I$ be such that $\operatorname{dist}(c',C)<\operatorname{dist}(c,C)$ and $c'\sim_i c$. Let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}=\ensuremath\mathcal{P}_i(c)$. Then by construction, $\operatorname{proj}_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}(d)=c'$ and there exists a minimal gallery $\gamma$ from $c'$ to $e$ through $d$ by the induction hypothesis. Minimality yields that also $\operatorname{proj}_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}(e)=c'$. Hence $\operatorname{dist}(c,e)>\operatorname{dist}(c',e)$ and the gallery obtained by prepending $c\sim_i c'$ to $\gamma$ is again minimal.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
Let $C$ be a panel-closed subset of $\Delta$ and let $c\in\Delta$.
    We will call the unique chamber $d \in C$ closest to $c$ the \emph{projection} of $c$ on $d$ and we will denote it by $\operatorname{proj}_C(c)$.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
    \item
        Let $c \in \Delta$ be a chamber. As in \cite[Definition 1.3]{silva1}, we define the \emph{ball} and the \emph{sphere} of radius $n$ around $c$ by
    	\begin{align*}
    		\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_n(c) &= \{d\in\Delta \mid \operatorname{dist}(c,d)\leq n\},\\
    		\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_n(c) &= \{d\in\Delta \mid \operatorname{dist}(c,d)= n\}.
    	\end{align*}
    \item
        More generally, let $C \subseteq \Delta$ be panel-closed. Then we define the \emph{ball} and the \emph{sphere} of radius $n$ around $C$ by
    	\begin{align*}
    		\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_n(C) &= \{d\in\Delta \mid \operatorname{dist}(C,d)\leq n\},\\
    		\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_n(C) &= \{d\in\Delta \mid \operatorname{dist}(C,d)= n\}.
    	\end{align*}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:C-spheres}
	\label{lem:panel-to-C}
	Let $C \subseteq \Delta$ be panel-closed and let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be an $i$-panel.
	Let $n$ be the smallest number such that $\ensuremath\mathcal{P} \cap \ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_n(C) \neq \emptyset$.
	Then either
	\begin{enumerate}[label={\rm (\alph*)}]
	    \item\label{lem:C-spheres:a} \begin{itemize}
	        \item $\ensuremath\mathcal{P} \subseteq \ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_n(C)$,
	        \item $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is parallel to a panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}' \subseteq C$, and
	        \item $\operatorname{proj}_C(\ensuremath\mathcal{P}) = \ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$; \quad or
	    \end{itemize} \vspace*{1ex}
	    \item\label{lem:C-spheres:b} \begin{itemize}
	        \item $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ has exactly one chamber in $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_n(C)$ and all its other chambers in $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_{n+1}(C)$,
	        \item $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is not parallel to any panel in $C$, and
	        \item $\operatorname{proj}_C(\ensuremath\mathcal{P}) = \{ e \}$ for some $e \in C$.
	    \end{itemize}
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Let $c \in \ensuremath\mathcal{P} \cap \ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_n(C)$. Since every other chamber in $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is adjacent to $c$, we already have $\ensuremath\mathcal{P} \subseteq \ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_n(C) \cup \ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_{n+1}(C)$.
    
	Assume that there is a second chamber $d \in \ensuremath\mathcal{P}\cap\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_n(C)$ with $d \neq c$.  If $\operatorname{proj}_C(c)=\operatorname{proj}_C(d) =: e$, then $\operatorname{proj}_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}(e)$ will be a chamber in $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_{n-1}(C)$ (because of the gate property applied to $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$), contradicting the minimality of $n$.
	Hence we must have $\operatorname{proj}_C(c)\neq\operatorname{proj}_C(d)$. Those projections are $i$-adjacent; let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ be the $i$-panel through them. By \cref{prop:parallelinrab}\ref{prop:parallelinrab:4}, $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ and $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ are parallel, and since $C$ is panel-closed, we have $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}' \subseteq C$.
	In particular, all chambers in $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ are at the same distance from $C$, so $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\subseteq\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_n(C)$.
	
	Assume now that $c$ is the only chamber in $\ensuremath\mathcal{P} \cap \ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_n(C)$, so that all its other chambers lie in $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_{n+1}(C)$.
	Since not all chambers of $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ lie at the same distance from $C$, the panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ can certainly not be parallel to any panel in $C$.
	In particular, \cref{prop:parallelinrab}\ref{prop:parallelinrab:4} now implies that all chambers in $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ must have the same projection on~$C$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:C-closingsquares}
    Let $C \subseteq \Delta$ be panel-closed.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item \label{lem:C-closingsquares:1}
            Let $c_1, c_2, c_3 \in \Delta$ be such that $\operatorname{dist}(C,c_1) = \operatorname{dist}(C,c_3) = n$, $\operatorname{dist}(C,c_2) = n+1$, and $c_1\sim_i c_2\sim_j c_3$ for $i\neq j$. Then $m_{ij}=2$ and there exists $d\in\Delta$ such that $\operatorname{dist}(C,d) = n-1$ and $c_1\sim_j d\sim_i c_3$.
        \item \label{lem:C-closingsquares:2}
            Let $c_1, c_2, c_3 \in \Delta$ be such that $\operatorname{dist}(C,c_1) = \operatorname{dist}(C,c_2) = n+1$, $\operatorname{dist}(C,c_3) = n$, and $c_1\sim_i c_2\sim_j c_3$ for $i\neq j$. Then $m_{ij}=2$ and there exists $d\in\Delta$ such that $\operatorname{dist}(C,d) = n$ and $c_1\sim_j d\sim_i c_3$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
        \item
            By \cref{lem:C-spheres}, the chambers $c_1$, $c_2$ and $c_3$ all have the same projection on~$C$.
            We can thus immediately apply \cref{lem:closingsquares}\ref{lem:closingsquares:1}.
        \item
            By \cref{lem:C-spheres}, the chambers $c_2$ and $c_3$ have the same projection $c$ on~$C$.
            Let $d := \operatorname{proj}_C(c_1)$.
            If also $d = c$, then we can apply \cref{lem:closingsquares}\ref{lem:closingsquares:2}.
            If $d \neq c$, then the $i$-panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ through $c_1$ and $c_2$ is parallel to the $i$-panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ through $c$ and $d$, which is contained in $C$ because $C$ is panel-closed.
            By \cref{prop:parallelinrab}\ref{prop:parallelinrab:2}, $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ and $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ are contained in a common residue of type $i \cup i^\perp$. In particular, the minimal gallery from $c_2$ to $c$ through $c_3$ is of this type, hence $j \in i^\perp$.
            
            Since $ij = ji$, there exists a chamber $d \in \Delta$ with $c_1 \sim_j d \sim_i c_3$.
            Let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}''$ be the $i$-panel containing $d$ and $c_3$. By construction, $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}''$ is parallel to~$\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$, but since parallelism is an equivalence relation (\cref{prop:parallelinrab}\ref{prop:parallelinrab:3}), this implies that $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}''$ and $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}' \subseteq C$ are also parallel. Since $\operatorname{dist}(C,c_3)=n$, this implies that also $\operatorname{dist}(C,d)=n$, and we have found the required configuration.
        \qedhere
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:C-concave}
    Let $C \subseteq \Delta$ be panel-closed and let $c_1, c_2 \in \Delta$. Then there exists a minimal gallery
    \[ \gamma = (v_0,\dots,v_\ell), \quad \text{with } v_0 = c_1,\ v_\ell = c_2, \]
    such that there are numbers $0 \leq j \leq k \leq \ell$ satisfying:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\operatorname{dist}(C, v_i) < \operatorname{dist}(C, v_{i-1})$ for all $i \in \{ 1,\dots, j \}$,
        \item $\operatorname{dist}(C, v_i) = \operatorname{dist}(C, v_{i-1})$ for all $i \in \{ j+1,\dots, k \}$,
        \item $\operatorname{dist}(C, v_i) > \operatorname{dist}(C, v_{i-1})$ for all $i \in \{ k+1,\dots, \ell \}$.
    \end{itemize}
    Such a minimal gallery from $c_1$ to $c_2$ will be called \emph{concave (with respect to $C$)}.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The proof from \cite[Lemma 2.11]{silva1} for the case $C = \{ c \}$ only relies on the closing squares lemmas. By \cref{lem:C-closingsquares}, the proof carries over \emph{mutatis mutandis} to the case where $C$ is any panel-closed subset of $\Delta$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:technicalprojectionstuff}
	Let $c \in \Delta$ and let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P} \subseteq \Delta$ be an $i$-panel. Let $c'=\operatorname{proj}_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}(c)$ and $\operatorname{dist}(c,c') = n$. Let $d\in\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_{n+1}(c)\setminus\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$, let $d'=\operatorname{proj}_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}(d)$, and assume that $d'\neq c'$, i.e., $d' \in \ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_{n+1}(c)$.
	
	Then $d'$ is $j$-adjacent to some chamber in $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_n(c)$ with $m_{ij}=2$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
This is \cite[Lemma 2.15]{silva1}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:convextechnicalprojectionstuff}
	Let $C \subseteq \Delta$ be panel-closed and let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be an $i$-panel as in \cref{lem:C-spheres}\ref{lem:C-spheres:b}, with $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\cap\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_n(C) = \{ c' \}$.
	Let $d\in\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_{n+1}(C)\setminus\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$, let $d'=\operatorname{proj}_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}(d)$, and assume that $d' \neq c'$, i.e., $d'\in\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_{n+1}(C)$.
	
	Then either $d$ is contained in an $i$-panel parallel to $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$, or $d'$ is $j$-adjacent to some chamber in $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_n(C)$ with $m_{ij}=2$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
By \cref{prop:C-concave}, there is a minimal gallery $\gamma = (d', e, \dots, d)$ from $d'$ to $d$ that is concave with respect to $C$.
    By concavity, either $e \in \ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_n(C)$, or all chambers of $\gamma$ lie in $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_{n+1}(C)$.
    If $e \in \ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_n(C)$, then the result already follows from \cref{lem:C-closingsquares}\ref{lem:C-closingsquares:1} applied on $c' \sim_i d' \sim_j e$.
    
    Assume now that all chambers of $\gamma$ lie in $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_{n+1}(C)$.
    We will show by induction on $\operatorname{dist}(d, \ensuremath\mathcal{P})$ that $d$ is contained in an $i$-panel parallel to $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$.
    Of course, this is obvious if $\operatorname{dist}(d, \ensuremath\mathcal{P}) = 0$, so assume $\operatorname{dist}(d, \ensuremath\mathcal{P}) \geq 1$, so that $e$ really exists. (If $\operatorname{dist}(d, \ensuremath\mathcal{P})= 1$, we set $e=d$.)
    We can now apply \cref{lem:C-closingsquares}\ref{lem:C-closingsquares:2} on $e \sim_j d' \sim_i c'$ to get $m_{ij} = 2$ and to find a chamber $e' \in \ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_n(C)$ with $e' \sim_i e$.
    In particular, $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is parallel to the $i$-panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ through $e$ and $e'$, and $\operatorname{dist}(d, \ensuremath\mathcal{P}') = \operatorname{dist}(d, \ensuremath\mathcal{P}) - 1$.
    We have $\operatorname{proj}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'}(d) = e$, and the subgallery $\gamma' = (e,\dots,d)$ of $\gamma$ is still a concave gallery completely contained in $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_{n+1}(C)$.
    Hence we can apply the induction hypothesis to find that $d$ is contained in an $i$-panel parallel to $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$.
    Since parallelism is an equivalence relation, the result follows.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\index{convex}
	\label{prop:evenmoretechnicalextensionstuff}
	Let $C \subseteq \Delta$ be panel-closed. Let $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ be local data over $I$, and let $g\in\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ be an automorphism mapping chambers in $C$ to harmonious chambers (with respect to $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$).
	
	Then there exists an automorphism $h\in\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ with the following properties:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\mathchoice{{g\bigr\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{g\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{g\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{g\rvert_{C}^{}}}=\mathchoice{{h\bigr\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{h\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{h\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{h\rvert_{C}^{}}}$;
		\item for each $i$ and for each $i$-panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$, either $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is parallel to a panel contained in~$C$, or we have $\sigma_\lambda(h,\ensuremath\mathcal{P})\in F_i$ (or both).
	\end{enumerate}
	Note that, in particular, $h$ maps all chambers in $\Delta$ to harmonious chambers.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
We will recursively construct a sequence of elements $g_n \in \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ such that $\mathchoice{{g_n\bigr\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{g_n\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{g_n\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{g_n\rvert_{C}^{}}}=\mathchoice{{h\bigr\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{h\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{h\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{h\rvert_{C}^{}}}$ for all $n$, such that property (ii) holds for all panels $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ contained in $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_n(C)$, and such that $g_n$ and $g_m$ agree on the ball $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_m(C)$ whenever $m<n$. Note that $g_n$ maps chambers in $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_n(C)$ to harmonious chambers. For $n=0$, take $g_0=g$.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            

	Now assume that $n\geq 0$ and that we have constructed $g_n$ with all the required properties. In order to define $g_{n+1}$, we will construct an automorphism $h_n$ that stabilizes $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_n(g_n\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax C)$ pointwise and that fixes the mismatching local actions at $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_{n+1}(g_n\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax C)$ --- we can then set $g_{n+1}=h_n\circ g_n$. Already let $C'=g_n\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax C=g\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax C$.
	
	For convenience, we will call a panel \emph{$n$-defective} if it intersects both $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_n(C)$ and $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_{n+1}(C)$  and it does not satisfy property (ii) with respect to $g_n$. Explicitly, if an $i$-panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is $n$-defective, then the local action $\sigma_\lambda(g_n,\ensuremath\mathcal{P})\notin F_i$ and $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is not parallel to any panel contained in $C$. Observe that, if property~(ii) holds for some panel, then it holds for every parallel panel as well, since parallelism is transitive and local actions on parallel panels agree. This implies that an $n$-defective panel cannot be parallel to any panel in $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_n(C)$.
	
	Let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be an $n$-defective $i$-panel. By \cref{lem:C-spheres}, $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ intersects $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_n(C)$ in a single chamber $c$. Let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'=g_n\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ and $c' = g_n\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax c$. By the induction hypothesis, $c$ and $c'$ are harmonious. Hence we can find a permutation $f_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\in F_i$ such that $f_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax\lambda_i(c)=\lambda_i(c')$, and a permutation $\pi_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ of the chambers in $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ that makes the diagram below commute.
	\[\begin{tikzcd}[dims={5em}{4em}]
		\ensuremath\mathcal{P} \ar[d,"\lambda_i",swap] \ar[r,"g_n"] &
			\ensuremath\mathcal{P}' \ar[r,"\pi_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}"] &
			\ensuremath\mathcal{P}' \ar[d,"\lambda_i"]\\
		\Omega_i \ar[rr,"f_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}"] && \Omega_i
	\end{tikzcd}\]
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          
	By \cite[Proposition 4.2]{caprace2014}, $\pi_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ extends to an automorphism $\widetilde\pi_\ensuremath\mathcal{P} \in \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ that fixes all chambers whose projection onto $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is fixed by $\pi_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$. Note that $\pi_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ fixes $c'$ by construction.
	Consider $d\in\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_{n+1}(C')\setminus\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ and denote $d'=\operatorname{proj}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'}(d)$. If $\operatorname{dist}(d',C')=n$, or in other words if $c'=d'$, then $d'$ is fixed by $\pi_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ and $d$ is fixed by $\widetilde\pi_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$. Otherwise $\operatorname{dist}(d',C')=n+1$. By \cref{lem:convextechnicalprojectionstuff}, $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ is parallel either to the $i$-panel containing $d$, or to an $i$-panel contained in $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_n(C')$. However, we have excluded the latter possibility by assuming that $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ violates property (ii).
	
	We have thus constructed, for every $n$-defective panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$, an auto\-morphism $\widetilde\pi_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ of the building with the property that all chambers of $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_{n+1}(C')$ that are moved by $\widetilde\pi_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ are contained in $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_{n+1}(C')\cap\ensuremath\mathcal{R}$, with $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}$ the set of all chambers in a panel parallel to $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ (in other words, the residue of type $i\cup i^\perp$ containing $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$).

	Next, we claim that no chamber in $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_{n+1}(C')$ lies in more than one $n$-defective panel. Indeed, suppose that $c_1\sim_i d\sim_j c_2$ with $d\in\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{S}}_{n+1}(C')$ and $c_1,c_2\in\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_n(C')$. Then by \cref{lem:C-closingsquares}\ref{lem:C-closingsquares:1}, the $i$-panel (and also the $j$-panel) through $d$ is parallel to a panel in $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_n(C')$, so that it cannot be $n$-defective.
	
	\medskip
	
	We now define
	\[h_n = \prod_\ensuremath\mathcal{P} \widetilde\pi_\ensuremath\mathcal{P} \in \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta),\]
	where the product runs over any set of arbitrarily chosen representatives of all equivalence classes of parallel $n$-defective panels, in an arbitrary order. Note that $h_n$ leaves invariant the set $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_n(C')$, since all factors do. In particular, the automorphism $g_{n+1}=h_n\circ g_n$ satisfies $\mathchoice{{g_{n+1}\bigr\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{g_{n+1}\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{g_{n+1}\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{g_{n+1}\rvert_{C}^{}}}=\mathchoice{{g_n\bigr\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{g_n\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{g_n\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{g_n\rvert_{C}^{}}}=\mathchoice{{g\bigr\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{g\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{g\rvert_{C}^{}}}{{g\rvert_{C}^{}}}$.
	
	Moreover, let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be any panel contained in $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_{n+1}(C)$. If $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\subseteq\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_n(C)$, then property (ii) holds by the induction hypothesis. If $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\subseteq\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_{n+1}(C)$, then $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is parallel to some panel contained in $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_n(C)$ and again property (ii) holds by induction. It only remains to verify that property (ii) is valid for an $n$-defective panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ with respect to $g_{n+1}$. Let $\widetilde\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be the representative of $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ in the class of parallel $n$-defective panels. Then
	\[\sigma_\lambda(g_{n+1},\ensuremath\mathcal{P})
		= \sigma_\lambda(g_{n+1},\widetilde\ensuremath\mathcal{P})
		= \sigma_\lambda(h_n,g_n\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax\widetilde\ensuremath\mathcal{P}) \circ \sigma_\lambda(g_n,\widetilde\ensuremath\mathcal{P})
		= \pi_{\widetilde\ensuremath\mathcal{P}} \circ \sigma_\lambda(g_n,\widetilde\ensuremath\mathcal{P})
		= f_{\widetilde\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}\in F_i.\]
	Finally, by construction, $g_{n+1}$ agrees with $g_n$ on the ball $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_n(C)$. The sequence of automorphisms $g_0,g_1,g_2,\ldots$ thus obtained, converges to an automorphism satisfying the desired properties.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The intuitive reason for the assumption that $C$ be panel-closed in the above proposition is the following: If a partial automorphism is defined on a nontrivial subset of a panel only, we would need to extend it to the full panel first. This would require us to assume the partial local actions to be extendable to a full permutation in the local group in the first place. Panel-closure is a sufficient assumption to get rid of this additional technicality.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{def:restricted1}
	Let $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ be a collection of permutation groups $F_i\leq\operatorname{Sym}(\Omega_i)$, indexed by $i\in I$. Then we define                                                                                        
	\begin{multline*}
	   \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) = \bigl\{g\in\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta) \bigm| \text{$\sigma_\lambda(g,\ensuremath\mathcal{P})\in F_i$ for every $i\in I$ and} \\
	       \text{\emph{all but finitely many} $i$-panels $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$}\bigr\}.
	\end{multline*}
	Note that by \cref{lem:localcomposition}, $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is closed under composition and inversion, and is hence a subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$. We clearly have inclusions
    \[ \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) \leq \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) \leq \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta) . \]
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
Let $g\in \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$. An $i$-panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ with $\sigma_\lambda(g,\ensuremath\mathcal{P})\notin F_i$ will be called a \emph{singularity} of $g$. We denote the (finite) set of all singularities of $g$ by $S(g)$.
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:locallyinfinitesingularities}
	Assume that $i,j\in I$ such that $m_{ij}=2$. If $q_j$ is infinite, then a panel of type $i$ can never be a singularity of an element $g\in\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Since the $i$-panels in a residue of type $\{i,j\}$ with $m_{ij}=2$ are parallel, this follows immediately from \cref{prop:parallellocals}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{def:ladder}
\begin{enumerate}
    \item 
    	A \emph{ladder} is a rank three building of type
    	\[M = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2\\ 2 & 1 & \mathclap{\infty}\\ 2 & \mathclap{\infty} & 1\end{pmatrix}
    	\qquad
    	\begin{tikzpicture}        
    		\path (0,0) node[myvertex] (B) {} +(.5,.75) node[myvertex] (A) {} +(1,0) node[myvertex] (C) {};
    		\draw[myedge] (B) -- node[above] {$\infty$} (C);
    	\end{tikzpicture} \quad . \]
    	The \emph{rungs} of a ladder are the panels of the type corresponding to the isolated node of the diagram. We have visualized the ladder's Coxeter complex in \cref{fig:coxeterladder}.
    \item 
    	A \emph{ladder of $\Delta$} is a residue of $\Delta$ that has the type of a ladder, and its \emph{rungs} will be the corresponding panels of $\Delta$. Clearly, a ladder always has infinitely many rungs.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:rungsnotsingular}
	Let $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}$ be a ladder in $\Delta$. Then a rung of\, $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}$ can never be a singularity of an element $g\in\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Since the rungs of a ladder are parallel, this follows immediately from \cref{prop:parallellocals}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:unboundedrungs}
	Let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be an $i$-panel of $\Delta$ such that the set of all panels parallel to $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is unbounded. Then $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is the rung of a ladder in $\Delta$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ be a panel such that $\operatorname{dist}(\ensuremath\mathcal{P},\ensuremath\mathcal{P}') \geq |I|$. Let $c\in \ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ and let $c'=\operatorname{proj}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'}(c)$. A minimal gallery $\gamma$ from $c$ to $c'$ has only types in $i^\perp$ (by \cref{prop:parallelinrab}) and has length $\operatorname{dist}(\ensuremath\mathcal{P},\ensuremath\mathcal{P}') > |i^\perp|$. By the pigeonhole principle, there is a type $j\in i^\perp$ that occurs at least twice in the type of $\gamma$. In between, there must exist a type $k\in i^\perp$ in $\gamma$ such that $m_{jk}=\infty$, since the type of $\gamma$ is a reduced word. Hence, we have found three types $\{i,j,k\}$ satisfying $m_{ij}=m_{ik}=2$ and $m_{jk}=\infty$, i.e., the $i$-panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is the rung of at least one ladder in $\Delta$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a simple, undirected graph. A vertex~$v$ of $G$ will be called a \emph{rung} if there exist two other, adjacent vertices $w_1\sim w_2$ in $G$ such that $v$ is adjacent to neither $w_1$ nor $w_2$. We call the graph $G$ \emph{ladderful} if every vertex is a rung.
	The right-angled diagram $M$ is called \emph{ladderful} if its underlying graph is ladderful.
	In \cref{fig:smallladderfulgraphs}, we have drawn all ladderful diagrams of rank $\leq 6$.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:ladderful}
    If $M$ is ladderful, then $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) = \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Since $M$ is ladderful, every panel of $\Delta$ is the rung of some ladder in $\Delta$.
    By \cref{lem:rungsnotsingular}, this implies that an element $g \in \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ cannot have any singularities at all.
    Hence $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) = \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:localinyoung}
	Let $g\in\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ and let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be a singularity of $g$ of type $i$. Assume that $i$ is not an isolated node of the diagram. Then at least one of the following holds:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item the local action $\sigma_\lambda(g,\ensuremath\mathcal{P})$ is contained in the Young overgroup $\widehat F_i$ of the local group $F_i$, or
		\item $F_i$ has at least two infinite orbits, while $F_j$ has finite degree for all $j\neq i$.
	\end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Assume that $\sigma = \sigma_\lambda(g,\ensuremath\mathcal{P})$ is not contained in $\widehat F_i$, so there exists a color $x\in\Omega_i$ such that $x$ and $\sigma\!\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax x$ are contained in \emph{different} $F_i$-orbits. Let $c\in\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be such that $\lambda_i(c)=x$, let $j\neq i$, and let $d$ be any chamber $j$-adjacent to $c$. Since $\lambda_i(c)=\lambda_i(d)$ and $\lambda_i(g\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax c)=\lambda_i(g\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax d)$, the $i$-panel containing $d$ is again a singularity. As there are only finitely many singularities, this implies that the parameter $q_j$ is finite, for every $j\neq i$.
	
	Next, we claim that both orbits $F_i\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax x$ and $F_i\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax(\sigma\!\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax x)$ are infinite. Assume by means of contradiction that $X = F_i\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax x$ is finite. Since $\sigma$ is a permutation and $x\in X$ with $\sigma\!\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax x\notin X$, there exists a color $y\notin X$ with $\sigma\!\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax y\in X$. Let $c'\in\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be such that $\lambda_i(c')=y$ and note that $c\neq c'$. Since $i$ is not an isolated node in the diagram, there exists some $k\in I$ with $m_{ik}=\infty$; choose $d\sim_k c'$. Since $\lambda_i(d) = \lambda_i(c') = y$ and $\lambda_i(g \mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax d) = \lambda_i(g \mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax c') = \sigma \mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax y$ are in different $F_i$-orbits, the local action at the $i$-panels containing $d$ is again a permutation not contained in~$\widehat F_i$. We can thus repeat this construction to obtain an infinite chain
	\[  c \sim_i c' \sim_k d \sim_i d' \sim_k \dotsm , \]
	every chamber of which lies in a singularity of type $i$. This contradiction shows that the orbit $F_i\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax x$ cannot be finite. Similarly, $F_i\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax(\sigma\!\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax x)$ cannot be finite.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:younggroupsinlocfincase}
	Assume that $\Delta$ is locally finite. Then we have an inclusion $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) \leq \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\widehat F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$, with $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\widehat F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ the local data obtained from the Young overgroups of the local groups in $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
This follows immediately from \cref{prop:localinyoung}.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{def:restricted2}
	Let $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ and $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ be two collections of local data for $\Delta$, satisfying
	\[F_i \leq \acute F_i \leq \widehat F_i \leq \operatorname{Sym}(\Omega_i)\]
	for every $i\in I$. In particular, $F_i$ and $\acute F_i$ have identical orbits.
	We define the \emph{restricted universal group} of $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ and $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ over $\Delta$ as
	\[\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) = \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) \cap{} \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}).\]
	In other words, $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is the group of all automorphisms that locally act like permutations in $F_i$ but with a finite number of exceptions for which the local action still follows a prescribed behavior, namely a permutation in $\acute F_i$. We will continue to refer to those exceptions as \emph{singularities}, i.e., a singularity of $g \in \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is an $i$-panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ such that $\sigma_\lambda(g,\ensuremath\mathcal{P})\in\acute F_i\setminus F_i$. The set of all singularities will still be denoted as $S(g)$.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
Restricted universal groups were first introduced by Adrien Le Boudec in \cite{leboudec} in the setting of trees. The name originates from \cite{caprace_dense}, where the authors remark the analogy with \emph{restricted direct products}. There are a few related constructions in the literature, but especially in topological group theory, the restricted direct product of a collection of groups $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$ with respect to subgroups $\{H_i\leq G_i\}_{i\in I}$ (over any index set $I$) is defined to be the subgroup
	\[ \Bigl\{ (g_i)_{i\in I}\in \prod_{i\in I} G_i \Bigm| \text{$g_i\in H_i$ for all but finitely many $i\in I$}\Bigr\}\]
	of the standard direct product. Just like the restricted direct product imposes additional constraints on all but finitely many factors, automorphisms in $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ are essentially automorphisms in $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ with additional constraints on all but finitely many panels.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:reducible}
	Let $\Delta$ be a reducible right-angled building over $I$. Let $J_1,\ldots, J_m$ be the connected components of the diagram with at least two nodes, and let $J$ be their union. Let $k_1,\ldots,k_n$ be the isolated nodes of the diagram, and let $K$ be their union.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item If $m=0$ (i.e., all nodes are isolated), then \[ \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) = \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) \cong \acute F_{k_1} \times {\cdots} \times \acute F_{k_n} . \]
		\item If $m=1$, then
		      \begin{align*}
		      \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})
				&\cong \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_J}(\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}},\,\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}) \times \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_K}(\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{K}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{K}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{K}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{K}^{}}}) \\
				&\cong \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_J}(\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}},\,\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}) \times F_{k_1} \times {\cdots} \times F_{k_n} ,
		      \end{align*}
			where $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_J$ and $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_K$ are residues of types $J$ and $K$, respectively.
		\item If $m\geq 2$, then \[ \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) = \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) \cong \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_1}\!\left(\textstyle\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{J_1}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J_1}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J_1}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J_1}^{}}}\right) \times {\cdots} \times \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_m}\!\left(\textstyle\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{J_m}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J_m}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J_m}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J_m}^{}}}\right) . \]
	\end{enumerate}
	In particular, if the diagram is reducible and has no isolated nodes, then $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) = \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
        \item If $m=0$, then $\Delta$ is a finite building so that all panels can be singularities at the same time, hence $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) = \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$.
        \item If $m=1$, then $\Delta$ is isomorphic to the direct product of an infinite building $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_J$ with a finite building $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_K$. Then, viewing the chambers of $\Delta$ as pairs of chambers in $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_J$ and $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_K$, we can identify $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ with a subgroup $H$ of $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_J}(\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}) \times \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_K}(\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{K}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{K}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{K}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{K}^{}}})$. Since $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_K$ is finite, each potential singularity $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ in $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_J$ corresponds to finitely many panels in $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_J \times \ensuremath\mathcal{R}_K$, hence $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_J}(\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}},\,\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}) \times 1$ is contained in $H$. It is obvious that also $1 \times \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_K}(\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{K}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{K}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{K}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{K}^{}}}) \leq H$, so we already get
            \[ \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_J}(\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}},\,\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}) \times \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_K}(\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{K}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{K}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{K}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{K}^{}}}) \leq H . \]
            Conversely, if $g \in H$, then no panel of $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_K$ can be a singularity for $g$ in $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_J \times \ensuremath\mathcal{R}_K$ because $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_J$ is infinite (or because it is contained in a ladder of $\Delta$), so the restriction of $g$ to $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_K$ is contained in $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_K}(\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{K}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{K}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{K}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{K}^{}}})$.
            It is obvious that the restriction of $g$ to $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_J$ is contained in $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_J}(\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}},\,\mathchoice{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\bigr\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}}{{\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}\rvert_{J}^{}}})$, and the conclusion follows.
        \item If $m=2$, then the diagram $M$ is ladderful, so by \cref{lem:rungsnotsingular}, we have $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) = \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$. It follows that
        \[ \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) = \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) \cap \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) = \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) \cap \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) = \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) . \qedhere \]
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:restrictedorbits}
	Two residues lie in the same orbit of $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ if and only if they are of the same type and harmonious.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
For each $i\in I$, the orbits of the local groups $F_i$ and $\acute F_i$ agree. By \cref{prop:universalorbits}, the same is true for the orbits of $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ and $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ on $\Delta$. Since $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})\leq\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})\leq\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$, the result now follows from the same \cref{prop:universalorbits}.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:restrictedlocallemma}
	Let $f$ be a permutation in $\acute F_i$ and let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be an $i$-panel. Then there exists an automorphism $g\in\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ with the following properties:
	\begin{enumerate}[label={\rm (\alph*)}]
		\item\label{lem:restrictedlocallemma:a} $g$ stabilizes $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$;
		\item\label{lem:restrictedlocallemma:b} the local action is equal to $f$ at every panel parallel to $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$;
		\item\label{lem:restrictedlocallemma:c} the local action is a permutation in $F_i$ at every other panel.
	\end{enumerate}
	If $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is not the rung of a ladder in $\Delta$, then $g\in\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
The permutation $f \in \acute F_i$ corresponds to a permutation $\tilde f \in \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}(\acute F_i)$.
	By \cref{prop:ext-res}, $\tilde f$ extends to an automorphism $h \in \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_\Delta(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$.
	We can now apply \cref{prop:evenmoretechnicalextensionstuff} with $C = \ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ as the convex panel-closed set to find the required $g \in \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ satisfying all three conditions.
	(Recall that by \cref{prop:parallellocals}, condition~\ref{lem:restrictedlocallemma:b} is automatically satisfied.)
	
	In particular, $g \in \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$.
	Moreover, if $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is not the rung of a ladder in $\Delta$, then by \cref{prop:unboundedrungs}, the set of panels parallel to $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is bounded and hence finite (because $\Delta$ is locally finite); it then follows that $g\in\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
\label{def:KnP}
	Let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be a panel of $\Delta$.
	\begin{enumerate}
        \item
            We define the subgroup
        	\[K_\ensuremath\mathcal{P} = \bigl\{g\in\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) \bigm| \text{$g$ stabilizes $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ and every singularity of $g$ is parallel to $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$} \bigr\}.\]
        	Notice that if $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is a rung in $\Delta$, then $K_P$ coincides with the panel stabilizer $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})_{\{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\}}$.
        \item
            For each integer $n\geq 0$, we define the subgroup
        	\[K_{n,\ensuremath\mathcal{P}} = \bigl\{g\in\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) \bigm| \text{$g$ stabilizes $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ and $\operatorname{dist}(\ensuremath\mathcal{P},\ensuremath\mathcal{P}')\leq n$ for every singularity $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$} \bigr\}.\]
	\end{enumerate}
	Note that both are indeed subgroups by \cref{lem:localcomposition}.
	(We do not include the local data $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ and $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ in the notation and hope that this will not cause any confusion.)
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:KPfromlocal}
	Let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be an $i$-panel that is not a rung in $\Delta$.
	\begin{enumerate}
	    \item\label{lem:KPfromlocal:1}
        	Let $f\in \acute F_i$ be a permutation. Then there exists an automorphism $g\in K_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ such that $\sigma_\lambda(g,\ensuremath\mathcal{P})=f$.
        \item\label{lem:KPfromlocal:2}
        	$\bigl[ K_\ensuremath\mathcal{P} \mathrel{:} \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})_{\{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\}}\bigr] = \bigl[ \acute F_i \mathrel{:} F_i\bigr]$.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
\Cref{lem:KPfromlocal:1} is a special case of \cref{prop:evenmoretechnicalextensionstuff}.
    By \cref{prop:parallellocals}, \ref{lem:KPfromlocal:2} now follows from \ref{lem:KPfromlocal:1}.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:restrictedcompgen}
	Let $\ensuremath\mathscr{H}$ be a set of representatives of harmonious panels of $\Delta$ that are not rungs. Then
	\[\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) = \bigl\langle \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}), K_\ensuremath\mathcal{P} \mid \ensuremath\mathcal{P}\in\ensuremath\mathscr{H}\bigr\rangle.\]
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Let $g\in\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$. We proceed by induction on the number $|S(g)|$ of singularities. Of course, if $S(g)=\emptyset$ then $g\in\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ and there is nothing to show, so assume that $\lvert S(g) \rvert \geq 1$ and let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be a singularity of type $i$. By \cref{lem:rungsnotsingular}, $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is not a rung in $\Delta$.
	
	By definition of $\ensuremath\mathscr{H}$, there is an $i$-panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}_0\in\ensuremath\mathscr{H}$ such that $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ and $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}_0$ are harmonious. By \cref{prop:universalorbits,prop:restrictedorbits}, there is thus an automorphism $h\in\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ such that $h\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax\ensuremath\mathcal{P}=\ensuremath\mathcal{P}_0$. By~\cref{prop:ext-res} applied on the residue $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$, we can assume that the local action of $h$ at $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is the identity. Next, let $\sigma = \sigma_\lambda(g,\ensuremath\mathcal{P})$. Using \cref{lem:KPfromlocal} we can find an automorphism $h_0\in K_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}_0}$ satisfying $\sigma_\lambda(h_0,\ensuremath\mathcal{P}_0)=\sigma^{-1}$.
	Finally, let $h' := h^{-1}\cdot h_0\cdot h \in K_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$.
	\[\begin{tikzcd}[dims={5em}{4em}]
		\ensuremath\mathcal{P} \ar[rrr,"h'"] \ar[dr,"h"] \ar[dd,"\lambda_i",swap]
			&&& \ensuremath\mathcal{P} \ar[dd,"\lambda_i"] \ar[r,"g"]
			& g\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax\ensuremath\mathcal{P} \ar[dd,"\lambda_i"]\\
		& \ensuremath\mathcal{P}_0 \ar[dl,"\lambda_i",swap] \ar[r,"h_0"]
			& \ensuremath\mathcal{P}_0 \ar[dr,"\lambda_i"] \ar[ru,"h^{-1}"]\\
		\Omega_i \ar[rrr,"\sigma^{-1}"]
			&&& \Omega_i \ar[r,"\sigma"]
			& \Omega_i
	\end{tikzcd}\]
	                                                  
	Consider the automorphism $g' = g\cdot h'$. By construction (see diagram), the local action of $g'$ at~$\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ is the identity. In particular, $g'$ does not have singularities parallel to~$\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$.
	
	Now let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ be any other panel that is not parallel to $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$; then $h'\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ is not parallel to $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ either. Since
	\[\sigma_\lambda(g',\ensuremath\mathcal{P}')
		= \sigma_\lambda(g,h'\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax\ensuremath\mathcal{P}') \circ \sigma_\lambda(h',\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'),\]
	where the second factor is known to be a permutation in $F_i$, we find that $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ is a singularity of $g'$ if and only if $h'\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ is a singularity of $g$.
	
	In other words, the number of singularities \emph{not parallel to $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$} is identical for $g$~and~$g'$; however, by the previous paragraph, $g$ has singularities parallel to $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ whereas $g'$ has none.
	This implies that $g'$ has strictly less singularities than $g$. The induction hypothesis finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:Hfinite}
    The set $\ensuremath\mathscr{H}$ in \cref{prop:restrictedcompgen} is finite. Indeed, denote the number of orbits of each local group $F_i$ by $m_i=\lvert\Omega_i/F_i\rvert$. Then by \cref{prop:restrictedorbits}, the action of $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ on the $i$-panels has $\prod_{j\neq i} m_j$ orbits. Summing over $i$,
    	\[ \lvert\ensuremath\mathscr{H}\rvert
    		= \sum_{\substack{i\in I \\ \textrm{not of rung-type}}} \prod_{j\neq i} m_j .
    		                                                        
    	\]
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:open-cont topology}
    Let $G$ be an abstract group containing a topological group $H$ as a subgroup.
    Then $G$ admits a unique group topology such that the inclusion $H \hookrightarrow G$ is continuous and open, provided that
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:open}
        gUg' \cap H \text{ is open in } H \tag{$*$}
    \end{equation}
    for all open subsets $U \subseteq H$ and for all $g,g' \in G$.
    
    Moreover, if $G$ is itself contained in a larger topological group $A$ in which $H$ is a closed subgroup (with the subgroup topology inherited from $A$), then this condition~\eqref{eq:open} is automatically satisfied.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
For the first statement, see \cite[Lemma 8.4]{neretingroups}.
    The second statement is now clear: if $U \subseteq H$ is open in $H$, then it is also open in $A$ and hence also $gUg'$ is open in $A$, so that $gUg' \cap H$ is indeed open in $H$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
\label{def:leboudectopology}
	For each choice of local data $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ and $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$, we endow $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ and $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ with the group topology obtained from \cref{lem:open-cont topology} using the embeddings $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) \hookrightarrow \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) \leq \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ and $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) \hookrightarrow \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) \leq \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$.
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
        \item 
            Since $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) = \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}) \cap \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$, the topologies on $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ and $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ are compatible, in the sense that $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is a closed subgroup of $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ (with the subspace topology).
        \item 
            Note that when $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}=\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$, the topology on $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})=\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ agrees with the permutation topology, but in general it does not. Indeed, in our topology on $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$, a subgroup $H\leq\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is open if and only if $H$ contains a pointwise stabilizer of a finite set of chambers \emph{intersected with $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$}. In other words, the topology on $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ in \cref{def:leboudectopology} is finer than the permutation topology.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:restrictedtdlc}
	Endow $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ with the topology from \cref{def:leboudectopology}.
	Then $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is a totally disconnected locally compact (tdlc) group.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
This follows immediately from the fact that $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is an open tdlc subgroup of~$\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ for this topology.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:restricteddiscrete}
	$\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is discrete if and only if every local group in $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ is free.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
By definition of the topology, $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is discrete if and only if $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is. The result is now an immediate consequence of \cite[Proposition 3.14]{bossaert}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:restrictedclosure}
	Let $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ and $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ be the local data over $I$ such that $F_i = \acute F_i$ for every $i\in I$ that is the type of a rung in $\Delta$.
	Then the closure of $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ in $\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ is $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Let $g\in\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$. It suffices to find a sequence of automorphisms $g_n\in\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$, where $n\in\mathbb N$, converging to $g$ in the permutation topology on $\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$. Let $c\in\Delta$ be any chamber and, for every $n\in\mathbb N$, define the set $B_n$ to be the convex closure of the ball $\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_n(c)$. Note that $B_n$ is panel-closed.
	
	\Cref{prop:evenmoretechnicalextensionstuff} yields an automorphism $g_n$ that agrees on $B_n$ with $g$. Moreover, the only panels where the local action of $g_n$ is not guaranteed to be a permutation in $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ are the panels parallel to some panel in $B_n$.
