By our assumption on the rungs, however, the parallel classes of singularities are bounded (\cref{prop:unboundedrungs}), and hence finite. Hence we have $g_n\in\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$, and this finishes our proof.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:restrictedboring}
	Let $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ and $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ be the local data over $I$ such that $F_i = \acute F_i$ for every $i\in I$ that is the type of a rung in $\Delta$.
	Then the following are equivalent:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}=\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$;                                      
		\item $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})=\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$;
		\item $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is closed in $\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$;
		\item chamber stabilizers of $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ are compact;
		\item chamber stabilizers of $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ are closed in $\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Implications (i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iii) $\Rightarrow$ (iv) $\Rightarrow$ (v) are straightforward. For (iii) $\Rightarrow$ (i), if $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is closed, then $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})=\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ by \cref{prop:restrictedclosure}, and hence $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}=\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$. Finally, (v) $\Rightarrow$ (iii) is a general fact in the permutation topology: if a point stabilizer of a permutation group is closed, then the group itself is closed.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:KPcompact}
	For each panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ of $\Delta$ and each integer $n \geq 0$, the subgroups $K_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ and $K_{n,\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}$ of $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ are compact open.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Since $K_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ contains the setwise panel stabilizer $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_{\{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\}}$ as a subgroup of finite index, it suffices to note that $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}_{\{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\}}$ is compact and open in $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ (as it is a union of finitely many cosets of chamber stabilizers), and hence in $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ as well. The same argument works for $K_{n,\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}$ once we note that the set $\{c\in\Delta\mid\operatorname{dist}(c,\ensuremath\mathcal{P})\leq n\}$ contains only finitely many panels.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:restrictedcompgen}
	The group $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is compactly generated.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
First, recall from \cite[Theorem 4.8]{bossaert} that $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is compactly generated.
	Combining \cref{lem:KPcompact,rem:Hfinite,prop:restrictedcompgen}, we now see that $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is generated by a finite number of compactly generated subgroups.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
A topological group is said to be \emph{regionally compact} if it is the increasing union of a family of compact open subgroups.
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
In the literature, regionally compact groups are also called \emph{locally elliptic}. The authors of \cite[Remark 1.0.1]{caprace_dense} argue why this terminology is best avoided: ``locally'' is suggestive of a property to be satisfied in some identity neighborhood basis, which is not the case here.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:panelstabregionallycompact}
	Let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be a panel of $\Delta$. Then the stabilizer $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})_{\{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\}}$ is regionally compact.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Since we can write
	\[ \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})_{\{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\}} = \mathop{\overrightarrow{\bigcup}}\displaylimits_{n\in\mathbb N} K_{n,\ensuremath\mathcal{P}} \,, \]
	the result follows immediately from \cref{lem:KPcompact}.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
A \emph{vertex cover} of a graph $\Gamma = (V, E)$ is a subset $W \subseteq V$ such that each edge $e \in E$ has at least one of its two vertices in $W$. A \emph{vertex cover} of the diagram $M$ is a vertex cover of its underlying graph (omitting the labels $\infty$).
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:Usimple}
    Let $\Delta$ be irreducible.
    Assume that not all local groups $F_i$ are free (or equivalently, that $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is non-discrete).
    Then the universal group $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is (abstractly) simply if and only if the local groups $F_i$ are generated by point stabilizers for all $i \in I$ and are transitive for all $i$ in some vertex cover of the diagram $M$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
This is \cite[Theorem 5.7]{bossaert}.
    Notice that the condition that not all local groups $F_i$ be free was erroneously omitted in \emph{loc.\@~cit.}, but is required to exclude the possibility that $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})^+ = 1$, in which case we have not been able to determine whether or not the discrete group $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is simple.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- definition-19: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
        \item 
        	Let $i\in I$. An equivalence class of parallel $i$-panels is called an \emph{$i$-tree-wall} of $\Delta$. By slight abuse of notation, we often identify an $i$-tree-wall $\ensuremath\mathcal{T}$ with the set of chambers $\{c\in\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\mid\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\in\ensuremath\mathcal{T}\}$.
        \item\label{def:treewalltree}
        	Let $V_1$ be the set of all $i$-tree-walls of $\Delta$, and let $V_2$ be the set of all residues of $\Delta$ of type $I\setminus\{i\}$. Define a bipartite graph $\Gamma_i$ with vertex set $V_1\sqcup V_2$, where an $i$-tree-wall $\ensuremath\mathcal{T}$ is adjacent to a residue $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}$ of type $I\setminus\{i\}$ if and only if $\ensuremath\mathcal{T}\cap\ensuremath\mathcal{R}\neq\emptyset$. We call this graph the \emph{$i$-tree-wall tree} of $\Delta$.
        	By \cite[Proposition 2.39]{silva1}, each tree-wall tree is indeed a tree.
        	Notice that the \emph{edges} of $\Gamma_i$ correspond to residues of $\Delta$ of type $i^\perp$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-19 -->
<!-- definition-20: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
        \item 
        	Let $J\subseteq I$ and let $c\in\Delta$ be a chamber. Then the set of chambers
    		\[X_J(c) = \{d\in\Delta \mid \operatorname{proj}_\ensuremath\mathcal{R}(d) = c\}\]
    		where $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}$ is the $J$-residue containing $c$, is called the \emph{$J$-wing of $c$}. If $J=\{j\}$ is a singleton, we simply write $X_j(c)$ and call it the \emph{$j$-wing of $c$}.
        \item 
        	For each chamber $c\in\Delta$ and each $i\in I$, we define the subgroup
        	\[
        		V_i(c) = \{g\in \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta) \mid \text{$g\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax d=d$ for all chambers $d\notin X_i(c)$}\} \leq \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta).
        	\]
        	Note that $V_i(c)$ fixes all chambers of the $i$-tree-wall containing $c$.
        	Moreover, for each subgroup $G \leq \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$, we will write
        	\[
        		V_i^G(c) = V_i(c) \cap G.
        	\]
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-20 -->
<!-- definition-21: body_md -->
\label{def:minimalbuilding}
	Let $G \leq \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item The action is \emph{cobounded} if there exists a constant $r\in\mathbb N$ and a chamber $c\in\Delta$ such that
			\[\Delta = \bigcup_{g\in G}\ensuremath\operatorname{\mathsf{B}}_r(g\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax c),\]
			i.e.,~if every chamber lies at a uniformly bounded distance to some $G$-orbit.
		\item The action is \emph{minimal} if $G$ leaves no nontrivial convex subset of $\Delta$ invariant.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                              
		\item The action is \emph{combinatorially dense} if it is minimal and moreover, for every $i\in I$, the induced action on the $i$-tree-wall tree $\Gamma_i$ has no fixed point at infinity.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-21 -->
<!-- definition-22: body_md -->
For each $i\in I$, define the \emph{$i$-distance} $\operatorname{dist}_i(c_1,c_2)$ between any two chambers $c_1$ and $c_2$ as the number of occurences of type $i$ in a minimal gallery joining $c_1$ and $c_2$. Note that this number does not depend on the chosen minimal gallery. This distance function is only a pseudometric, since chambers in a common residue of type $I\setminus\{i\}$ are at $i$-distance zero.
<!-- end definition-22 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:quasiisometricaldistances}
	Let $c_1$ and $c_2$ be any two chambers of $\Delta$. Let $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_1$ and $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_2$ be the residues of type $i^\perp$ containing $c_1$ and $c_2$ respectively, viewed as edges in the $i$-tree-wall tree $\Gamma_i$. Then
	\[\operatorname{dist}_{\Gamma_i}(\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_1,\ensuremath\mathcal{R}_2) = 2\cdot\operatorname{dist}_i(c_1,c_2)+\epsilon \leq \operatorname{dist}(c_1,c_2),\qquad\text{where }\epsilon\in\{-1,0,1\}.\]
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
The inequality is clear. For the equality, pick any minimal gallery $\gamma$ from $c_1$ to $c_2$ in $\Delta$ and consider the induced path in the $i$-tree-wall tree, which is a path without backtracking. Notice that we have a one-to-one correspondence between $i$-adjacencies on $\gamma$ on the one hand, and pairs of adjacent edges in $\Gamma_i$ sharing a common vertex in the bipartition class of residues of type $i\cup i^\perp$ on the other hand. Consequently, if the path in $\Gamma_i$ has even length, say $2n$, there are $n$ adjacencies of type $i$ on $\gamma$, and if the path has odd length, say $2n+1$, there are either $n$ or $n+1$ adjacencies of type $i$ on $\gamma$. Our conclusion follows.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:cobounded-TWT}
	Let $G \leq \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$.
	If the action of $G$ is cobounded, then its induced action on each tree-wall tree $\Gamma_i$ is also cobounded.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
This is an immediate consequence of \cref{lem:quasiisometricaldistances}.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:coboundeddense}
		Let $G \leq \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ and assume that the diagram $M$ has no isolated nodes. If the action of $G$ is cobounded, then it is combinatorially dense.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
The fact that the action of $G$ is \emph{minimal} was already shown in \cite[Lemma 4.5]{bossaert}.
	Now let $i\in I$ and consider the $i$-tree-wall tree $\Gamma_i$. By \cref{cor:cobounded-TWT}, the induced action of $G$ on $\Gamma_i$ is also cobounded. Note that $\Gamma_i$ is unbounded, as $i$ is not an isolated node of the diagram. If $G$ would fix a point at infinity $\xi$ of the $i$-tree-wall tree, then it would stabilize all \emph{horospheres} through $\xi$. However, for each horosphere, there are vertices of the tree at unbounded distance to that horosphere, contradicting the coboundedness.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:combinatorially dense}
    Assume that the diagram $M$ has no isolated nodes.
    Then the universal groups $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ and the restricted universal groups $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ are combinatorially dense.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
It suffices to observe that already $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\mathbf{1})$ is cobounded (where $\mathbf{1}$ is the local data with $F_i = 1$ for all $i$), as in \cite[Corollary 3.4]{bossaert}, so also any larger subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ is cobounded. The result now follows from \cref{lem:coboundeddense}.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{prop:minimalcharacterisations}
	Let $G \leq \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ and assume that the diagram $M$ has no isolated nodes. Then the following are equivalent:
	\begin{enumerate}[label={\rm (\alph*)},leftmargin=6ex]
		\item the action of $G$ on $\Delta$ is minimal;
		\item for each $i\in I$, the induced action of $G$ on the $i$-tree-wall tree $\Gamma_i$ is minimal.
	\end{enumerate}
	As a corollary, the following are equivalent:
	\begin{enumerate}[label={\rm (\alph*)},leftmargin=6ex]
		\item the action of\, $G$ on $\Delta$ is combinatorially dense;
		\item for each $i\in I$, the induced action of $G$ on the $i$-tree-wall tree $\Gamma_i$ is combinatorially dense.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
First assume $G$ does not act minimally on $\Delta$, i.e., there exists a nontrivial convex $G$-invariant subset $C$ of chambers. Let $c\sim_i d$ be such that $c\in C$ and $d\notin C$. Using absence of isolated nodes in the diagram, take $j\in I$ such that $m_{ij}=2$, and let $e\sim_j d$. By convexity, $e\notin C$. Now define $C'$ as the set of vertices in $\Gamma_i$ that correspond to residues of $\Delta$ having nonempty intersection with $C$,
	\[C' = \bigl\{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}\in\operatorname{Res}_{I\setminus\{i\}}(\Delta) \bigm| \ensuremath\mathcal{R}\cap C \neq \emptyset\bigr\}
		\cup \bigl\{\ensuremath\mathcal{R}\in\operatorname{Res}_{\{i\}\cup\{i\}^\perp}(\Delta) \bigm| \ensuremath\mathcal{R}\cap C \neq \emptyset\bigr\}.\]
	Note that $C'$ is a nonempty $G$-invariant subtree of $\Gamma_i$. Moreover, we claim that $e$ is not contained in any residue in $C'$. Indeed, if it were the case that $e\in\ensuremath\mathcal{R}\in C'$, let $e'\in \ensuremath\mathcal{R}\cap C$. The projection $\operatorname{proj}_\ensuremath\mathcal{R}(c)$ is either $d$ or $e$, depending on the type of~$\ensuremath\mathcal{R}$. By the gate property, there is a minimal gallery joining $c$ to $e'$ passing through either $d$ or $e$, contradicting the convexity of $C$. Hence, $C'$ is a \emph{nontrivial} $G$-invariant subtree, and the action of $G$ on $\Gamma_i$ is not minimal.
	
	Conversely, assume that $G$ does not act minimally on $\Gamma_i$ for some $i\in I$, i.e.~there exists a nontrivial $G$-invariant subtree $D$. Define $D'$ as the set of chambers of $\Delta$ that lie in a residue corresponding to a vertex in $D$,
	\[D' = \bigl\{c\in\Delta \bigm| \text{$c\in\ensuremath\mathcal{R}\in D$ for some residue $\ensuremath\mathcal{R}$ of type $I\setminus\{i\}$ or type $\{i\}\cup \{i\}^\perp$}\bigr\}.\]
	Clearly $D'$ is a nontrivial $G$-invariant subset of chambers. Let $c,c'\in D'$ and consider a minimal gallery $\gamma$ from $c$ to $d$ in $\Delta$. Then $\gamma$ descends to a path in~$\Gamma_i$ between the residues in $D$ containing $c$ and $d$. This path is contained in the subtree~$D$, hence $\gamma$ is contained in $D'$. In other words, $D'$ is a nontrivial \emph{convex} $G$-invariant subsystem, and the action of $G$ on $\Delta$ is not minimal.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{prop:normaltreedense}
    Let $T$ be a tree and $G \leq \operatorname{Aut}(T)$.
    If $G$ is combinatorially dense, then so is any non-trivial normal subgroup $N \unlhd G$.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
This is \cite[Lemme 4.4]{tits_arbres}.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:combdensenormal}
	Assume that the diagram $M$ is irreducible. Let $G \leq \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ be combinatorially dense and let $N\unlhd G$ be a nontrivial normal subgroup. Then also the action of $N$ on $\Delta$ is combinatorially dense.
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
The subtle but important point here is that because $\Delta$ is irreducible, the induced action of $\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ on each tree-wall tree $\Gamma_i$ is \emph{faithful}; see \cite[Lemma~3.19]{silva1}.
    In particular, the action of $N$ on each $\Gamma_i$ is non-trivial.
	The result now follows from \cref{prop:minimalcharacterisations,prop:normaltreedense}.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- definition-23: body_md -->
Let $T$ be a tree and let $g \in \operatorname{Aut}(T)$.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item We call $g$ an \emph{inversion} if $g$ inverts some edge of $T$.
        \item We call $g$ \emph{elliptic} if $g$ fixes a vertex.
        \item We call $g$ \emph{hyperbolic} otherwise, in which case there is a bi-infinite path $\gamma$ in $T$ left invariant by $g$ and on which $g$ induces a non-trivial translation. We call $\gamma$ the \emph{axis} of $g$.
    \end{enumerate}
    In particular, if $G \leq \operatorname{Aut}(T)$ acts \emph{without inversion} (i.e., $G$ fixes the bipartition of the vertex set of $T$), then each element of $G$ is either elliptic or hyperbolic.
<!-- end definition-23 -->
<!-- definition-24: body_md -->
Let $g \in \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ and let $i \in I$.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item We call $g$ \emph{$i$-elliptic} if the induced action of $g$ on $\Gamma_i$ is elliptic.
        \item We call $g$ \emph{$i$-hyperbolic} otherwise. The axis $\gamma$ for the action of $g$ on $\Gamma_i$ will be called the \emph{$i$-axis} of $g$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-24 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{prop:magictreestuff}
    Let $T$ be a tree and let $G \leq \operatorname{Aut}(T)$ act without inversion. Assume that the action is combinatorially dense.
    Let $e_1,e_2$ be two edges of $T$.
    Then there exists a hyperbolic element $g \in G$, the axis $\gamma$ of which contains both $e_1$ and $e_2$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
We may of course assume that $e_1\neq e_2$. Let $T_1$ be the half-tree determined by $e_1$ not containing $e_2$ and let $T_2$ be the half-tree determined by $e_2$ not containing $e_1$. By \cite[Lemma 4.3]{leboudec}, there exist two hyperbolic elements $g_1$ and $g_2$ in $G$ with axes $\gamma_1 \subset T_1$ and $\gamma_2 \subset T_2$, respectively. In particular, the axes are disjoint, and the shortest path joining $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ passes through both $e_1$ and $e_2$. The product $g_1 g_2$ is then the required hyperbolic automorphism; its axis will contain this shortest path.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
\label{hyperbolic}
	\label{lem:normalsubcontainshyperbolics}
	Assume that the diagram $M$ is irreducible. Let $i\in I$ and let $e_1,e_2$ be adjacent edges of the $i$-tree-wall tree $\Gamma_i$. Let $N\unlhd G$ be a nontrivial normal subgroup and assume that the action of $G$ on $\Delta$ is combinatorially dense. Then $N$ contains an $i$-hyperbolic automorphism, the axis of which contains both $e_1$ and $e_2$.
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
By \cref{lem:combdensenormal}, the action of $N$ on $\Delta$ is combinatorially dense.
	By \cref{prop:minimalcharacterisations}, the induced action of $N$ on $\Gamma_i$ is combinatorially dense, so we can apply \cref{prop:magictreestuff}.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- definition-25: body_md -->
Let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be an $i$-panel and let $\ensuremath\mathcal{T}$ be the corresponding $i$-tree-wall.
	Let $G \leq \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ and let $G_{(\ensuremath\mathcal{T})}$ be the pointwise stabilizer of the set of all chambers in $\ensuremath\mathcal{T}$.
	For each $c\in\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$, we define the morphism
	\[\varphi_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P},c}\colon G_{(\ensuremath\mathcal{T})}\to V_i(c),
		\quad\text{with }
		\varphi_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P},c}(g)\colon\Delta\to\Delta\colon d\mapsto\begin{cases}
			g\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax d & \text{if $d\in X_i(c)$;}\\
			d & \text{otherwise.}
		\end{cases}\]
	The proof of \cite[Proposition 5.2]{caprace2014} shows that $\varphi_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P},c}(g)$ is indeed an automorphism of $\Delta$, which is clearly contained in $V_i(c)$, but not necessarily in $V_i^G(c)$.
	We say that $G$ satisfies the \emph{independence property} when for each panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$, each chamber $c \in \ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ and each $g \in G$, the automorphism $\varphi_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P},c}(g)$ is again contained in $G$ (and hence in $V_i^G(c)$).
	If this is the case, then for each panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$, the elements of $G$ can be decomposed into ``independent'' elements acting on each of the wings:
	\[
	   \varphi_\ensuremath\mathcal{P} \colon G_{(\ensuremath\mathcal{T})} \xrightarrow{\sim} \prod_{c\,\in\,\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}  V_i^G(c) \colon g \mapsto \prod_{c\,\in\,\ensuremath\mathcal{P}} \varphi_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P},c}(g) .
	\]
<!-- end definition-25 -->
<!-- proposition-19: body_md -->
\label{prop:restricteduniversalindependence}
	$\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ satisfies the independence property.
<!-- end proposition-19 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
Let $G = \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$, let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be an $i$-panel, let $\ensuremath\mathcal{T}$ be the corresponding $i$-tree-wall and let $c \in \ensuremath\mathcal{P}$.
	Let $g \in G_{(T)}$ and $h = \varphi_{\ensuremath\mathcal{P},c}(g) \in \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$.
	To show that $h \in G$, we will follow the proof of the independence property for $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ from \cite[Proposition 3.16]{silva1}, with as only new ingredient the fact that we have to allow a finite number of singularities.
	More precisely, if some $j$-panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ is contained in $\ensuremath\mathcal{T}$ or in any of the other $i$-wings $X_i(d)$ with $d \neq c$, then $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ is fixed by $h$; in particular, it cannot be a singularity.
	On the other hand, if $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ is contained in the $i$-wing $X_i(c)$, then the local action of $h$ on $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$ coincides with the local action of $g$ on $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}'$, which, by assumption, is contained in $F_j$ up to a finite number of exceptions, for which it is contained in $\acute F_j$.
	This shows that indeed $h \in \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:auxnormaltreewall}
	Let $G \leq \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$.
	Let $i\in I$ and let $c$ and $d$ be two chambers in a common $i$-panel $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ of $\Delta$. Let $g\in G$ and assume that $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ and $g\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ are not parallel, that $\operatorname{proj}_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}(g\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax c)=d$ and that $\operatorname{proj}_{g\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}(d)=g\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax c$. Consider an automorphism
	\[b\in\prod_{e\,\in\,\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\setminus\{c,d\}} V_i^G(e).\]
	Then there exists an automorphism $h\in G$ such that $b=[h,g]$.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
The proof of \cite[Lemma 3.17]{silva1} can be copied \emph{verbatim} to this more general setting.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- proposition-20: body_md -->
\label{prop:normaltreewall}
	Let $\Delta$ be irreducible and let $G \leq \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$. Assume that $G$ is combinatorially dense. Let $N\unlhd G$ be a nontrivial normal subgroup. Then $N$ contains $V_i^G(c)$ for all $i \in I$ and all chambers $c \in \Delta$.
	
	In particular, if $G$ also satisfies the independence property, then $N$ contains the fixator $G_{(\ensuremath\mathcal{T})}$ of every $i$-tree-wall $\ensuremath\mathcal{T}$\!.
<!-- end proposition-20 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Let $\ensuremath\mathcal{T}$ be an arbitrary $i$-tree-wall and let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be an $i$-panel of $\ensuremath\mathcal{T}$\!. In the $i$-tree-wall tree $\Gamma_i$, $\ensuremath\mathcal{T}$ corresponds to a vertex $v$ and the edges incident to $v$ correspond to the chambers in $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$. Let $c,d$ be two distinct chambers of $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$. By \cref{lem:normalsubcontainshyperbolics}, there exists some $i$-hyperbolic element $g\in N$ such that the axis of $g$ in $\Gamma_i$ contains the two edges corresponding to $c$ and $d$. We can assume that $d$ is the chamber pointing towards the attracting end of $g$ in $\partial\Gamma_i$ and $c$ towards the repelling end, replacing $g$ by $g^{-1}$ if necessary.
	
	Note that $g\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax\ensuremath\mathcal{T}\neq\ensuremath\mathcal{T}$ since $g$ is an $i$-hyperbolic automorphism. Moreover, by construction, we have $\operatorname{proj}_\ensuremath\mathcal{P}(g\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax c)=d$ and $\operatorname{proj}_{g\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax\ensuremath\mathcal{P}}(d)=g\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax c$. Hence we can apply \cref{lem:auxnormaltreewall} to obtain that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:Vi}
	   \prod_{e\,\in\,\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\setminus\{c,d\}} V_i^G(e) \subseteq N. \tag{$\ast$}
	\end{equation}
	Since $\Delta$ is assumed to be thick, there is at least one such chamber $e\,\in\,\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\setminus\{c,d\}$. Now recall that $c$ and $d$ were chosen arbitrarily in $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$, so we can repeat the proof with different pairs $\{c,d\}$ and multiply the resulting equations \eqref{eq:Vi} to obtain that 
	\[ \prod_{e\,\in\,\ensuremath\mathcal{P}} V_i^G(e) \subseteq N. \]
	Moreover, if $G$ satisfies the independence property, then $G_{(\ensuremath\mathcal{T})} = \prod_{e\,\in\,\ensuremath\mathcal{P}} V_i^G(e)$, showing the last statement.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- proposition-21: body_md -->
\label{prop:restricteduniversalmonolithic}
	Let $\Delta$ be irreducible and let $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ be local data such that not all local groups $F_i$ are free. Then $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is monolithic; the monolith is the subgroup $N$ generated by all tree-wall fixators.
	Moreover, $N$ is simple.
<!-- end proposition-21 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Write $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}} = \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ and $N = \langle \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_{(\ensuremath\mathcal{T})} \rangle$, where $\ensuremath\mathcal{T}$ ranges over all tree-walls. Note that $N$ is nontrivial, since not all local groups act freely. Thanks to \cref{cor:combinatorially dense,prop:restricteduniversalindependence}, we may apply \cref{prop:normaltreewall} to obtain that every normal subgroup of~$\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$ contains $N$. Hence $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$ is monolithic with monolith $N$.

	To show that $N$ is simple, let $A\trianglelefteq N$ be the intersection of all nontrivial normal subgroups of $N$. This is a characteristic subgroup of $N$, which is therefore normal in~$\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$.
	Notice that $N$ is combinatorially dense by \cref{lem:combdensenormal}, so by \cref{prop:normaltreewall} (applied with $N$ in place of $G$), any nontrivial normal subgroup of $N$ contains $V_i^N(c)$, for all $i \in I$ and all $c \in \Delta$. It follows that also $A$ contains all $V_i^N(c)$.
	Now recall that $V_i^{\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}}(c) \leq \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_{(\ensuremath\mathcal{T})} \leq N$ (where $\ensuremath\mathcal{T}$ is the $i$-tree-wall through $c$), so $V_i^N(c) = V_i^{\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}}(c) \neq 1$.
	
	It follows that $A$ is a nontrivial normal subgroup of $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$.
	By \cref{prop:normaltreewall} again, $A$ contains the monolith $N$, so that in fact $A=N$, showing that $N$ is indeed simple.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- proposition-22: body_md -->
Assume that the diagram $M$ is irreducible and not ladderful.
	Then every nontrivial normal subgroup of $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is open.
	In particular, $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is topologically simple if and only if it is abstractly simple.
<!-- end proposition-22 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Write $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}} = \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$.
	If every local group $F_i$ acts freely, then $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$ is discrete and there is nothing to prove.
	
	Otherwise, $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$ is monolithic by \cref{prop:restricteduniversalmonolithic} and the monolith is generated by tree-wall fixators. By the assumption on the diagram, there exists at least one index $i\in I$ such that an $i$-tree-wall~$\ensuremath\mathcal{T}$ contains only finitely many chambers. Then the fixator $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_{(\ensuremath\mathcal{T})}$ --- as the intersection of finitely many chamber stabilizers --- is open. Consequently, the monolith of $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$ is open, and so is every non\-trivial normal subgroup of $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- proposition-23: body_md -->
\label{prop:genbychamstab}
	Assume that $M$ has no isolated nodes. The following are equivalent.
	\begin{enumerate}[label={\rm (\alph*)}]
		\item\label{prop:genbychamstab:a} $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})^+=\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$;
		\item\label{prop:genbychamstab:b} $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})^+$ has finite index in $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$;
		\item\label{prop:genbychamstab:c} the local groups are generated by point stabilisers for every $i\in I$, and are transitive for every $i$ in some vertex cover of (the underlying graph of) the diagram of $\Delta$.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-23 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
This is \cite[Theorem 5.6]{bossaert}, except that statement \ref{prop:genbychamstab:b} is not mentioned in the statement of \emph{loc.\@~cit.} but only in its proof, more precisely in the first paragraph on p.\@~884.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:restrictedvirtsimple}
	Let $\Delta$ be a thick irreducible right-angled building over an index set $I$ with $\lvert I \rvert \geq 2$. Let $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ and $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ be the local data as in \cref{def:restricted2}. Assume that $F_i = \acute F_i$ for every $i\in I$ that is the type of a rung. Moreover, assume that not all local groups $\acute F_i$ are free.            
	
	Then the restricted universal group $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ is virtually simple if and only if $\acute F_i$ is generated by point stabilizers for every $i\in I$ and transitive for every $i$ in some vertex cover of the diagram of $\Delta$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
Abbreviate $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}} = \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{F}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{},\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$ and $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}} = \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{})$.
	First, suppose that $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$ has a simple subgroup $H$ of finite index. Since $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$ is infinite, $H$ is a normal subgroup of $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$.
	On the other hand, by \cref{prop:restricteduniversalmonolithic}, $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$ is monolithic, with monolith $N = \langle \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_{(\ensuremath\mathcal{T})} \rangle$, where $\ensuremath\mathcal{T}$ ranges over all tree-walls. Since $N \leq H$ and $H$ is simple, we have $N = H$, so the monolith $N$ of $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$ has finite index in $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$.

	Now let $A = \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}^+ \cap \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}} \unlhd \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$.
	By \cref{prop:restrictedclosure}, $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$ is dense in $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}$. Since $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}^+$ is an open subgroup of $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}$, it follows that $A \neq 1$. Hence $A$ has finite index in~$\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$.
	 Taking the closure, it then follows that $\overline{A}$ has finite index in $\overline{\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}} = \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}$. Since $\overline{A} \leq \overline{\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}^+} \cap \overline{\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}} = \operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}^+$, we see that $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}^+$ has finite index in $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}$, and the characterisation follows from \cref{prop:genbychamstab}.

    \medskip
    
	Conversely, suppose that the local data $\ensuremath\boldsymbol{\smash{\acute F}}\@ifnextchar,{\mkern-2mu}{}$ satisfies the assumptions postulated. Then by \cref{thm:Usimple}, $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}$ is simple. Let $N = \langle \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_{(\ensuremath\mathcal{T})} \rangle$ be the open normal subgroup of $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$ generated by all fixators of tree-walls $\ensuremath\mathcal{T}$ of $\Delta$. By \cref{prop:restricteduniversalmonolithic}, $N$ is a simple group and it is the monolith of $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$. We will show that $N$ has finite index in~$\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$.
	
	The closure of $N \leq \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ is a normal subgroup of $\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}$. Hence $N$ is dense in~$\operatorname{\mkern2mu\mathcal{U}}$, and consequently in $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$ as well. This implies that the $N$-orbits and $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$-orbits on the building $\Delta$ agree: for any $c\in\Delta$ and $g\in\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$, the stabilizer $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_c$ is open, hence the intersection $N \cap {g\cdot\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_c}$ is nonempty, and any automorphism $h$ in the intersection satisfies $h\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax c= g\mkern 2mu\relax.\mkern 2mu\relax c$. It follows that $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}} = {\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_c}\cdot N$.
	
	Let $\ensuremath\mathcal{P}$ be a panel of $\Delta$. By the previous paragraph, $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}} = {\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_{\{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\}}}\cdot N$. Together with \cref{prop:panelstabregionallycompact}, we obtain an increasing union
	\[\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}} = \mathop{\overrightarrow{\bigcup}}\displaylimits_{n\in\mathbb N} H_n \cdot N,\]
	where the $H_n \leq \operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}_{\{\ensuremath\mathcal{P}\}}$ are compact open subgroups. On the other hand, $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$ is compactly generated by \cref{cor:restrictedcompgen}. The family $\{H_n \cdot N\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ defines an open cover of any compact generating set and hence $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}} = H_n\cdot N$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$.
	
	In conclusion, $N$ is both open and cocompact in $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$. The coset space ${\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}}/N$ being both compact and discrete, it follows that indeed $N$ has finite index in $\operatorname{\mkern1mu\mathcal{G}}$, which concludes our proof.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
